title: St Bartholomew's Day (1572)
hookLine: Protestants killed in Paris; religion used for massacre

lines: A WEDDING MEANT TO MAKE PEACE.
cards: In Paris, the Catholic king's sister marries the Protestant king of Navarre, a match meant to help end years of fighting between French Catholics and French Protestants, who were called Huguenots.
Protestant nobles come to the city to celebrate. Soon after, on the feast of the apostle Bartholomew, the killing starts. First the Huguenot leaders.
Then neighbors turn on neighbors in the streets, and the violence spreads to other towns. A day on the church calendar, named for one of the twelve, becomes the name of a massacre.

teach.h: KILLED BY THOSE WHO SHARED THEIR LORD.
teach.b: Historians still argue about who gave the orders, and how much was planned and how much was a mob let loose. What isn't in doubt: people were killed for their faith by people who said they shared the same Lord.

In the wars of religion that tore at France, both Catholics and Protestants killed, and both were killed. St Bartholomew's Day is the one whose name stuck. And this exact temptation shows up in the Gospels.
In Luke, a Samaritan village turns Jesus and his friends away.

teach.h: FIRE FROM HEAVEN? HE REBUKES THEM.
teach.b: James and John ask if they should call down fire from heaven to destroy it. In the King James Bible: "But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of."

And on the night of his arrest, when one of his followers draws a sword to defend him (John's Gospel names him as Peter), Jesus says, in Matthew: "Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword."
His own followers, reaching for violence on his behalf, and both times he says no.
That's where today's line comes from: never in his name. It isn't a line about other people's faiths. It's one Christians can turn on their own story, honestly, without pretending it didn't happen.
Remembering a day like this isn't about blame across the centuries. It's about recognizing the moment a faith starts to be used as a weapon, so the sword goes back in its place.

how: Christians of different churches remember the massacre in histories, sermons and services of repentance and reconciliation, and pray for places where religion is used to justify violence.

games.q: you're one of Jesus' disciples. a Samaritan village has just turned you away. what do you do?
o: ask him to call down fire on the village.
argue with the villagers until they let you in.
games.why: James and John asked for fire. Jesus turned and rebuked them, and the group went on to another village.

practice: Bring to mind one place where religion is being used for violence, and don't sort out the blame; just hold the people, the afraid, the grieving, even the ones holding the weapons.
If you pray, pray for that place, or rest with put up again thy sword into his place; if you don't, keep it in your attention, with care.

wordCard.voice: Huguenots. The French Protestants who were massacred first in Paris on St Bartholomew's Day, in a killing that came to stand for faith used as a weapon.

orig.note: Greek: sword, the word in Matthew 26:52 when Jesus tells the follower who drew it to put it away.

carryVoice: Your line: never in his name. A hard day to remember, and worth remembering. Rest well.
